explication:
<explanation>
1. Project Type & Purpose  
   • Mayo is a cross‑platform desktop application (Windows, Linux, macOS) plus a command‑line utility for viewing and converting 3D CAD files.  
   • Written in modern C++ using Qt for UI, OpenCascade for CAD kernel, and various 3rd‑party libraries (fmt, GSL, fast_float, magic_enum, etc.).  

2. File Structure Analysis  
   – Top‑level CMakeLists.txt, README and LICENSE define build and documentation.  
   – “src” subdivides into:  
     • app: main GUI application, window management, commands, dialogs, widgets.  
     • gui: view controllers, document wrappers, event handling.  
     • cli: command‑line interface entry point and export commands.  
     • base: core engine – document model, I/O registration, task management, settings, messaging.  
     • graphics: wrappers around OpenCascade’s rendering, scene/driver management.  
     • io_*: one directory per file format plugin (STEP, IGES, STL, OBJ, glTF, PLY, DXF, etc.).  
     • measure: measurement tools for geometry.  
     • qtbackend & qtcommon: glue between core engine and Qt (settings storage, translators, threading, string conversion).  
     • 3rdparty: bundled external libs (fmt, fast_float, GSL, etc.).  
   – i18n, images, docs and scripts support internationalization, icons/themes, user manual, build and release automation.  
   – tests folder contains unit tests spanning app, base, measure.

3. Key README Insights  
   – Emphasis on two front‑ends (GUI + CLI) over a shared core.  
   – Plugin‑style I/O system supporting import/export of many CAD formats.  
   – Architectural cues: modularity, extensibility, MVC‑style separation, command pattern.

4. Diagram Construction  
   a. Components  
      1. Front‑ends:  
         • GUI Application (src/app + src/gui + Qt backend)  
         • CLI Application (src/cli)  
      2. Core Engine (src/base):  
         • Document Manager, Task Manager, Settings, Messaging, I/O System Registry  
      3. I/O Plugins (src/io_*): one module per file format, registered with I/O System  
      4. Graphics Engine (src/graphics + OpenCascade): scene graph, object drivers, view controllers  
      5. Measurement Tools (src/measure)  
      6. Qt Integration Layer (src/qtbackend, src/qtcommon)  
      7. 3rd‑Party Libraries (fmt, GSL, fast_float, magic_enum, OpenCascade, Qt)  
      8. Build & CI: CMake, scripts, GitHub Actions  

   b. Relationships & Data Flows  
      • GUI ↔ Core: UI drives document creation, invokes commands, listens to engine events  
      • CLI → Core: issues batch export commands via I/O System  
      • Core ↔ I/O Plugins: Core hands over file read/write requests to registered plugins  
      • Core ↔ Graphics Engine: Core updates scene, issues render/update calls  
      • Measurement ↔ Core/Graphics: measurement tools query geometry from Core, overlay results in Graphics  
      • Qt Integration: GUI & Core communicate over Qt signals/slots; settings persisted via Qt backend  
      • 3rd‑Party: All layers depend on Qt and OpenCascade; core may use fmt/GSL/fast_float  

   c. Architectural Patterns  
      • Layered Architecture – Front‑ends, Core, Plugins, External libs  
      • Plugin Pattern – I/O modules dynamically registered  
      • MVC/MVP – GUI widgets (view) separate from app_context & document (model)  
      • Command Pattern – user actions mapped to commands_api  
      • Observer/Event Bus – messaging and Qt signals/slots for decoupling  

   d. Technologies & Frameworks  
      • Build: CMake, custom scripts, GitHub Actions pipelines  
      • UI: Qt Widgets, .ui forms, qrc resources, i18n via Qt Linguist  
      • CAD kernel: OpenCascade (BREP, mesh, XDE)  
      • Logging & formatting: fmt  
      • Utility libraries: GSL, fast_float, magic_enum  

5. Tailoring Diagram to Mayo  
   – Emphasize two front‑end entry points (GUI and CLI) pointing to a shared Core Engine.  
   – Within Core, highlight the I/O plugin registry and the document/task management subsystems.  
   – Show Graphics Engine as a self‑contained layer invoked by Core and connected to UI through Qt.  
   – Illustrate extensibility: adding a new src/io_<format> module simply plugs into the I/O System.  

6. Diagramming Guidelines  
   • Use clear boxes for each component or module (group source dirs).  
   • Draw directional arrows for data/control flow (e.g., GUI → Core → I/O Plugins → File System).  
   • Color code layers:  
     – Front‑ends (blue), Core (green), Plugins (orange), External Dependencies (gray).  
   • Use different shapes or dashed outlines for:  
     – Core services vs. plugins vs. third‑party libraries.  
   • Label connections with protocol or API used (e.g., “registerPlugin()”, “readModel()”, “renderScene()”).  
   • Annotate key patterns (e.g., “Observer: Qt signals/slots”, “Command Bus”).  

By breaking Mayo into these clearly labeled, color‑coded layers—front‑ends, core engine, I/O plugins, graphics, measurement, Qt integration, and external libs—and showing the direction of interactions and data flow, you will capture its full architecture and extensibility surface in a single, comprehensive system‐design diagram.
</explanation>
